props.title: The Night of the Hunter
props.initialSlug: Deranged preacher hunts children for hidden money

sections.content: **The Night of the Hunter** (1955) stands as one of cinema's most haunting Southern Gothic nightmares. Charles Laughton's only directorial effort crafts a twisted fairy tale about corrupt preacher Harry Powell (Robert Mitchum) hunting two children for hidden money. The film's German Expressionist-inspired visuals - particularly the iconic underwater shot of a murdered woman's hair swaying like seaweed - influenced directors from Martin Scorsese to Spike Lee. Mitchum's "LOVE" and "HATE" knuckle tattoos became an indelible piece of film iconography, referenced in works like **Do the Right Thing** (1989) and **The Blues Brothers** (1980).

sections.content: The film's lasting impact on thriller and horror cinema cannot be overstated. Its DNA runs through **Blue Velvet** (1986), where David Lynch similarly peeled back small-town Americana to reveal darkness underneath. The children-on-the-run sequence influenced **Pan's Labyrinth** (2006) and **A Quiet Place** (2018), while the predatory preacher character echoes through **There Will Be Blood** (2007) and **True Grit** (2010).

Cinematographer Stanley Cortez, who also shot **The Magnificent Ambersons** (1942), created a chiaroscuro nightmare that influenced horror's visual language for decades. The stark shadows and tilted angles appear in everything from **Carnival of Souls** (1962) to **The Texas Chain Saw Massacre** (1974). The film's blend of horror and childlike innocence laid groundwork for **The Spirit of the Beehive** (1973) and **Let the Right One In** (2008). SUBHEAD: Religious Horror Evolution

sections.content: **The Night of the Hunter** (1955) established the template for religious horror that would later flourish in films like **The Exorcist** (1973) and **Children of the Corn** (1984). Its exploration of corrupted faith influenced **Frailty** (2001) and **Saint Maud** (2019), while its portrayal of religious manipulation echoes through **Red State** (2011) and **The Witch** (2015).
